Yes, they do matter; but they are not problems that we will solve with this bill. I should like to talk about this bill, why we are taking this position and why I believe it is not wise to adopt any other procedure without taking into account at this stage which positions of the parties are just and which are not, because I do not think this body has been or is constituted in order to solve this type of problem. This does not mean that the unions are wrong. It does not mean that the railways are abusing the employees. It just means we are not in a position to pass judgment on the merits of the question. We have not been set up for that.
Just to give a short history, Mr. Chairman, we might consider how wages, outside of interventions of government in respect of minimum wages and regulations, are set in Canada. The general rule is through free collective bargaining in which the employers try to get together with the unions. If they do not get together, of course, there is a strike or a walkout. This is the general rule.
How is the level of wages established? Is it according to a certain rule of justice, as I heard yesterday? No. It is according to the strength of each party. I have been in that trade all my life. I was involved in certain strikes where the justice of the cause was very clear, and we lost. I was involved in others where it was less evident, and we won. Why? Because we were weak in the first case and strong in the second. This is the way disputes are settled. They are not settled according to certain criteria or principles known or accepted by everybody. It is free bargaining. In certain cases and in certain provinces there is what is called compulsory arbitration. What we call the right to strike has been removed, or is never given. Elsewhere we have what is called binding arbitration. This is where a judge says this is or is not the truth, and the problem is solved in that way.
Many strikes in this country have gone on for months and months. I think some have lasted as long as seven or eight months. Parliament has never been convened nor have any provincial assemblies been convened in these cases. The fight has been carried on in the streets in an effort to reach an agreement. Why are we here dealing with this problem? We are here because of the very nature of the activities of the railways. When there is a strike, it is not only the employers and the employees who are fighting one against the other; the public is involved. Here, as a government, we must try to find a procedure whereby the public does not suffer. This is the only reason. The right to strike is not at stake at the moment. We may discuss it at another time.
I notice that all parties, including the NDP, agree we should do something to compel the men to go back to work. Everybody recognizes it is the duty of parliament to send the men back to work. Even in the proposals of the NDP which I have seen, this is included. Of course, the

conditions may differ. This is what we should discuss. If the NDP had really adopted a socialistic attitude, they would have been opposed to any kind of settlement legislated by this House.

As a third responsibility, we must demand from the government a comprehensive program that will deal effectively with the cost of living and restore some stability and order to the economic life of this country. I emphasize these matters at this time because they are all part of a piece. These three responsibilities must be met by this parliament. They must be met quickly. If this government thinks that parliament will settle for anything less, or that Canadians will accept anything less, the government is in for a shock as well as a shaking.
Surely we did not come here to order others back to work and then go back on holiday ourselves. We are not here just to deal with this emergency situation, although that is our first priority. Surely, Sir, it would be an act of brazen callousness for this government to run away from its responsibilities, and it would be a faint-hearted parliament-indeed, a chicken parliament-that would let the government get away with it if that is what the government tried to do. We are here to get the trains moving again, but we are not here just to get the trains moving again-we are here to try to get the country moving again in the right direction.
I realize that having parliament in session at the end of August instead of on October 15 will create some discomfort and in some quarters some danger and difficulty. There is the discomfort of the government being confronted by parliament as further reports are forthcoming from Statistics Canada on the cost of living or on unemployment conditions in the country. There is the discomfort, if not the inconvenience, of the government being obliged to produce legislation, announce its plans and reveal its intentions to parliament. That is very, very much a part of the emergency that we are discussing here today. Presenting such a program may be a difficult thing to do, especially when there is no legislation and no plan. But the presence of parliament can serve as the conscience of the government and perhaps even as an inspiration to the government.
We are here to face our responsibilities in the public interest. I have outlined three of them. Of course, I believe-and I know that more and more Canadians are subscribing to the belief-that parliament has another responsibility as well, a responsibility to deny continued confidence to a government that sits on its hands, very content with itself, while the most serious bout of inflation psychology in recent memory takes hold and wreacks its terrible consequences. My party will accept that responsibility too, and there will come a time shortly for a test of confidence. The government cannot put that off too long. In the meantime, we will deal with our responsibilities in priority as we see them.
Our first responsibility and the first priority of this House, the legislation dealing with the railway dispute, is a matter that summons feelings of disappointment and regret, I know, for all members of the House. An interven-

tion of this kind is an occasion that must have a deeply sobering effect on anybody who values our system and our institutions, as I am sure the Minister of Transport does. We are faced with this responsibility because, as the minister recognizes, the broader public interest demands our action to meet a national emergency.
Members of my party have agreed to support such action, but we will not support what we feel is insupportable in regard to the interests of simple justice to the workers who will be affected by the actions we take. In the course of the present non-ops dispute one new technique, the technique of selective strike action, was attempted. As a variation of the rotating strike approach applied to the national railway system it was indeed something new to be tried on the side of labour. We were prepared to see this new approach given a trial, and we simply demanded that the government accept its responsibility to move the process to mediation and then to use the office of the Minister of Labour in seeking a settlement. The minister, as it turned out, ended up generating something new in labour relations himself. For the first time we had the spectacle of a windmill tilting at people. That, of course, is beside the point now. The point is that a new approach, could not in fact be maintained and events again brought us where we are today, taking emergency action after the fact and after enormous damage has been done. Let us resolve not to keep following this futile and damaging script in the future. The integrity of parliament itself demands nothing less than a change.

This was emphasized very effectively yesterday by the hon. member for St. John's East, namely, that we are not here to write a new contract for those involved; we are here to deal with this emergency and provide a basis upon which the railways can again start to operate.
On the matter of further negotiations, we feel that a realistic and firm time limit should be imposed with regard to negotiations, bargaining and arbitration. The parties in the dispute are near accord on a number of items which make up the collective agreement, so this should work no hardship. In the public mind, the imposition of such specific deadlines in the bill would have an appearance of orderliness.

My understanding is that the representatives of the union feel it would be a waste of time to be sent back to the bargaining table when, after being there a long time, they have not made any progress. There should be a definite limit on the time in which the bargaining can be strung out. We will, therefore, be moving an amendment to include in the bill a specification of durations for the ongoing periods of negotiation and mediation.
If developments proceed to the point of having an arbitrator appointed by cabinet, we feel there should be an opportunity for review and debate by parliament of the developments that have ensued to that point. Accordingly, we wish to see in this bill a clause such as was in the 1966 bill. This would provide such an opportunity. That clause provides for ten members of parliament bringing about a discussion following the appointment of an arbitrator by the minister or by cabinet. This is not a novel suggestion; it was in the 1966 bill.
On the matter of wages, we are not negotiating an agreement but, rather, back to work terms as the hon. member for St. John's East emphasized yesterday. He expressed the principle that governs the amendments we will propose. That principle involves building into the bill a protection to ensure that any settlement adequately takes into account increases in the cost of living as they can be more realistically projected since the time the members of the conciliation board drafted their reports earlier this year. In imposing a settlement, this parliament can do nothing less than provide that kind of insurance.

When I broke off at one o'clock I was emphasizing again, as some others have done, that we are not engaged here in working out a final settlement of the dispute but that we are, rather, involved in proposing a floor below which any final settlement may not go. I was emphasizing that such a floor must be a realistic one so that it would not have an adverse effect on attitudes of trust and good will which are necessary to set the stage for a satisfactorily negotiated final settlement.
Parliament, through the actions and the policies of the government of the day, does bear a responsibility for the general economic position of the country. With conditions as they now exist with regard to the cost of living and the escalation of the cost of living, parliament cannot simply pass the buck to the parties in the dispute, or to a mediator or arbitrator, without some clear expression and direction of the matters for which parliament is responsible, that is to say, the cost of living. This is particularly necessary when we are dealing with an imposed floor, that is, a floor proposed by parliament, an imposed back to work arrangement covering a two-year agreement. With the cost of the living picture as it is today, the amendments we will put forward are designed to see that parliament accepts its responsibility in this regard.
With respect to the second year of the contract term proposed in the bill, we will attempt to assure some cost of living protection by putting forward an amendment which would instruct an arbitrator to produce a final settlement which could be no lower than the percentage floor set by the legislation, plus a revised cost of living projection component based upon the most recent figures available to the arbitrator when the matter comes to arbitration. This would involve some consultation between the arbitrator and the members of the original conciliation board to ascertain the cost of living components which were in their recommendations as they relate to the second year. It is my recollection that for the year 1973 they were working on a basis of a cost of living factor of about 4 or 5 per cent; but I am now talking about the second year, the year 1974.
We are disturbed that in the bill as it now stands there is a better second year floor for the shopcrafts and the UTU than is provided for the non-ops. As a union might see it, there is a poorer second year provision for the non-ops than there is for the shopcrafts and the UTU. Surely if we are concerned about fairness and the necessity to avoid unnecessary bitterness, we cannot allow the bill to become law in the form in which it presently stands, particularly as it is the non-ops who would sustain the loss of recourse to strike action under the law as it now exists. To give them a lesser, or poorer arrangement for the second year than their brothers in the other two

August 31, 1973
Railway Operations Act
bargaining groups would seem to me to be a travesty of justice.
The shopcrafts and the UTU are provided a floor of 6lA per cent and 1V2 per cent for the second year, an effective average increase in the second year of 714 per cent over the first year. The non-ops, on the other hand, are provided with a floor of 5 per cent and an additional 3 per cent for the second half of the year, an effective average increase of 6 Vi per cent for the year 1974 as opposed to the 714 per cent proposed for the other two unions. The floor provided in the bill for the first year is essentially the same in respect of the three unions, except that in the case of the non-ops it is in cents whereas in the case of the other two unions it is in percentages. So it is evident that the non-operating unions are offered in this bill as it now stands a floor that is lower than for the other two, and this should be changed. Our proposal, in the form of an amendment, would call for the second year floor for the non-ops to be as good or no worse than the floor for the other two unions, and this would involve 6 'A per cent and IV2 per cent for the non-ops.

That is hardly a question, Mr. Chairman. I recognize this does involve some departure from the recommendation of the chairman, and I do not want to be critical of Mr. Justice Munroe, but I should point out that while the judge said he was awarding a 17 per cent increase to the non-ops over two years, that is correct if you compare the December 31, 1974, rate he recommended with the average non-ops wage for the year 1972, but if you compare the December 31, 1974, rate as he recommended with the December 31, 1972, rate it is only about 15 per cent.
I do not want to get involved in the recommendations of the chairman of the conciliation board in respect of the non-ops arrangement, but I am saying that this House should not impose a poorer settlement for the second year on the non-operating unions then we are providing for the other two unions, regardless of what difference there might be in the recommendations of the chairman of the conciliation board.
Actually, as the minister well knows, the scale of pay for the other two unions is substantially higher than for the non-operating unions, and even the same percentage increase gives them more in terms of dollars. The bill the minister puts before the House not only gives less in terms of dollars but a lower percentage increase, and I do not think he can justify that. I hope the minister will accept my point of view in that regard. The point I was making is

that we have to propose as good an arrangement for the non-operating unions for the second year as we are prepared to give the other two unions. I emphasize that fact.
In summary, the effect of our proposal in relation to the floor for the second year, 1974, would see a floor for all workers involved in the legislation of 6 Vi per cent and 1 Vi per cent, which is no worse than provided for the shopcrafts and UTU, plus a revised cost of living component to be determined by an arbitrator. We frame the cost of living aspect in terms of a direction to an arbitrator simply because this is the most simple and efficient method of inserting the principle into the bill. In other words, if the principle and the resulting improved floor are guaranteed to be available at the end of the ongoing negotiation line, they will automatically be presumed all along the line.
What we shall propose is that the percentage increase for the year 1974 should be no worse for the non-operating unions than the government is prepared, as indicated in the bill, to allow the other two unions, plus instructions to the arbitrator with regard to the cost of living component for the second year.
As to the first year, 1973, which we are now over halfway through, we consider we should continue to apply the principle that the cost of living component should be included. This was emphasized by the Minister of Transport this morning as being something which would have to be considered in the course of negotiation or arbitration. I am proposing that we are far enough along in the year 1973 to assess this ourselves for the year, rather than leaving it to arbitration and negotiation. In line with the principle I have expressed, we are far enough along in the year now for parliament to set its own revised cost of living component and make it part of the defined floor in this legislation. The board of conciliation worked on the basis of the cost of living factor in 1973 being close to 5.5 per cent. Clearly, the cost of living factor for 1973 will be about 1 per cent above that, and 1 per cent in terms of these average wages would amount to about 4 cents.
Therefore, in line with this principle which has been generally endorsed but which the government wishes to leave to conciliation and arbitration, we believe we are far enough along now in the year for parliament to assess this itself. We feel we should realistically establish the floor at 34 cents, and that this figure should replace the 30-cent floor figure which is now in the bill. I say that recognizing that the escalation of the cost of living will be about 1 per cent higher than the figure on which the board worked.
I emphasize that such action could in no way be construed as taking sides or attempting to make a final settlement judgment here in parliament. This would simply be parliament, in this case, accepting its responsibility in regard to the extraordinary cost of living situation which now prevails in the country.
I also assure the House that there is nothing intended in my approach to be considered as engaging in an auction. I agree wholeheartedly with the Minister of Transport that we should not be in an auction game in this House. At the same time, I appreciate that the government is virtually bound to bring in a bill in line with the recommendations of the chairman of the conciliation board and this is what the government has done. At the same time, I have heard

both the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport say they are assuming that a final settlement would have to take into account, regardless of any other components, some component of adjustment for the rising cost of living over and above the floor figure now in the bill. I would hope, therefore, that these ministers and indeed all members of the House will be able to support our amendments giving effect to an assurance of such an additional cost of living component in the final form of this legislation.
With regard to the other two unions, the increases there in the first year are in percentage terms, and that would have to be left to further conciliation and eventually arbitration if it comes to that. I am suggesting that for the non-ops, for 1973, we recognize the fact that the cost of living escalated faster than envisaged at the time of the conciliation report. Above all, I am emphasizing that the floor we propose for the non-operating unions should be no worse than the arrangements we propose for the other two unions.
We feel these proposals would have a salutary effect on the employees concerned. Surely this is a very important consideration both in ensuring an orderly return to work and setting the stage for ongoing negotiations. We believe that parliament would be doing no more than it should, in line with its limited role at this time, in supporting our amendments. We also believe that in doing so it will be doing what it indeed must do in the interests of justice in imposing a settlement at this time. These amendments will be presented formally, in detail, as the committee stage proceeds.

My friends need not indulge in that kind of discourtesy. They know that in committee of the whole one can speak times without number, and some of us are capable of it. But I do want to say a few words on the subject of railway pensions, which was my main purpose when I rose this morning and unsuccessfully sought the floor.
Yesterday in his speech the Minister of Labour announced the appointment of Dr. John Deutsch as commissioner, under part V of the Canada Labour Code, to study a certain aspect of railway pensions. We welcome this appointment and we approve of the person who has been named to do this job. We are pleased that that action has been taken. But I want to register a strong complaint at the narrowness of the terms of reference given to Dr. Deutsch and I appeal to the minister either to give him another set of terms of reference or, if he wants to give it to some other person, to appoint another commissioner.
Let me try to express this as quickly and as directly as I can. The job which the Minister of Labour has given to Dr. Deutsch is simply to assess the cost or the value of the pension changes that have been agreed to between the unions and the companies, the unions claiming that they represent a cost factor of 2.2 per cent, the companies claiming that they represent 4.3 per cent. This is a dispute that certainly should be settled by an independent person, and we find Dr. Deutsch to be such an independent person. I hope that if he finds in favour of the unions, or if he finds a figure somewhere in between, the terms of reference of the commission are such that the advantage thereof will be given to the workers in the wage settlement.
Mr. Chairman, that is not enough at this stage of the game with respect to railway pensions. I know the minister said yesterday that the pension agreement arrived at between the union and the company is an historic one, and so on. I know there is a lot to be said for it, but there are two things that stand out as deficiencies. In the first place, for some of those now at work, some of those not yet on pension, I do not think the deal is as good as it is claimed
Railway Operations Act
to be. This applies especially to the old timers, especially to those who were working for either of the major railways prior to January 1, 1956.
The new 2 per cent per year formula is there for those whose entire employment has been since 1956. I am not going for the moment into the Canada Pension Plan arrangements, which raise other questions, but for those whose employment goes back to a time prior to January 1, 1956, there is a deficiency. They will not get a pension of 2 per cent for each year of service. So I say quickly, but say it to have it on the record, that I do not share the complete satisfaction of the minister and some of the union representatives with respect to the deal so far as the present workers are concerned.
There is another group we must think of, those already retired, or those who were retired at any time prior to January 1, 1963. For them there is nothing at all in this pension agreement. There is not even any guarantee that the 2 per cent ad hoc increase that Canadian National has been giving from year to year will continue to be given. So this whole area of railway pensions, Canadian National, Canadian Pacific and those of any other companies that are in the group, needs to be gone into thoroughly by a man like Dr. Deutsch or some appointee who is given the same kind of job. I see the minister getting to his feet.
May I spell out one or two things. I suggest that either Dr. Deutsch's terms of reference should be broadened or that additional terms of reference should be given to someone else. Mr. Chairman, we have listened with interest and attention to the opinions expressed in this House since the beginning of the special debate on the railway dispute and it leaves us perplexed.
The present situation throughout Canada requires-we agree unanimously on that-immediate action on the part of the federal government. The economic situation is so much more precarious that several other major problems are involved and are creating discontent, tensions, strikes and even sometimes anger and violence throughout Canada.
The House has been summoned to an emergency session to force 56,000 workers of the Canadian National Railways to return immediately to work, thus taking away from them the right to strke that the same Parliament had given them previously. Parliament had given the right to strike to the workers in the public sector. Yet every time that the situation grows worse, that the negotiations do not produce results, that we come to a dead end, an emergency law, a special law is adopted by the House to take away their right to strike and force them to return to work. Instead of improving, and this is specially the point I would like to make, the mechanism of negotiation, instead of promoting permanent negotiations of labour agreements, instead of establishing in advance a labour tribunal or a permanent arbitration mechanism, and on this question I differ with the Leader of the Opposition

(Mr. Stanfield), representing fairly all the different interests, the government, for reasons which are of course obscure or political, gives the right to strike to the public sector, lets the situations rot to the point that they create a national crisis requiring emergency legislations and then in the same breath, takes away the right to strike.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to object strenuously against that philosophy of the working world, those evasive procedures of the present government before labour problems in general. I demand a long-term labour policy governed not only by a proper up-to-date labour code, but especially through permanent bargaining mechanisms for the renewal of collective agreements and above those mechanisms a labour court representing the various interests involved and this, Mr. Chairman, not only to solve the problems of the CNR employees but also those existing in other sectors of the public service where public interest is more often threatened.
The basic reasons which led to the introduction of the legislation are evidently plausible: the rotating strike since July 26 has shaken up the Canadian community. However, since August 23, this national strike, as mentioned by the minister, has jeopardized the welfare of the nation by isolating the Maritimes, let alone the many manufactures and companies which have been compelled to dismiss hundreds of employees since they were unable to obtain their raw materials.
Through this bill, Mr. Chairman, we shall force back to work 56,000 Canadian workers who were on strike because both bargaining and arbitration had failed. These workers are asking for a wage increase in order to meet the high cost of living. This is what they are fighting for. Must they be blamed for that? Is the government acting both as judge and employer? To this question fraught with consequences, I shall answer in the affirmative and the negative. Let me explain.
These 56,000 workers are not to blame, not any more than a great many other workers who are fighting with patched-up means, namely the strike, to secure a better income to support their families. They are not to blame because they want to improve their condition. But, under the present system where renewable collective agreements ahve been left to sleep on shelves for a long time instead of being seriously negotiated on a permanent basis, what else can they do?
Mr. Chairman, to my mind, that is the point. If, in the Labour Code, in the mechanisms of the labour world, we had a permanent system of labour negotiations to renew agreements instead of letting them gather dust on shelves for the benefit of private interests, we would not get into the type of difficult situation we are now witnessing.
How much will the work stoppage have cost each one of the railroaders who struck in order to improve their lot? How much will the settlement give them? Was it a profitable endeavour? If I worked for the railroads, if I saw this sitting of the House where in turn hon. members suggest 5 per cent, 3 per cent and 30c. increases, I would be disappointed because those workers are trying to tailor their salaries to the cost of living which is now beyond control.
This House should have but one objective: not only to enable the 56,000 employees of the Canadian railways to
Railway Operations Act
tailor their income to the cost of living, but to take steps to ensure that all Canadian workers can do so.
Mr. Chairman, finally, whose interests does this situation serve? Through rotating and full-scale strikes, the workers inadvertently served the interests of finance.
As long as governments tolerate the old-fashioned mechanisms of the world of labour, workers, regardless of what sector they belong to, will run into crying injustice, at times provocation, endless tugs-of-war and especially, constant failures.
Mr. Chairman, here is an important question upon which I urge my colleagues to reflect: Have you ever seen a Canadian worker emerge as a winner in the present bargaining system? Have you ever seen a worker emerge as a winner in the present financial system, in spite of his efforts?
That brings me to say, Mr. Chairman, that the public enemy No. 1, the one that is not talked about in this House, is the omnipresent world of finance that plays around with people like puppets, making them laugh or cry as they wish, dividing them among themselves, setting them up against imaginary enemies when the combines, the monopolies, the big companies-often multinational-protected by governments that indeed they finance continue to dominate our economic, social and consequently political life.
Mr. Chairman, that is the truth. Why do we let labour disputes last so long? Why is it, Mr. Chairman, that companies do not do more in the bargaining process? Why do governments wait until the last moment to intervene? Why do we not bring our bargaining, mediation and arbitration system up to date?
Mr. Chairman, if the 56,000 workers currently involved as the thousands of others in Canada put as much sustained effort in fi7/sting the present financial system, in fighting high finance as they do in gaining a few cents an hour after months of pressure, wild talks and strikes we would see that the result would not be the same as today.
I will give an example that I consider most important and which is relevant to the subject matter we are discussing. It has to do with the present strike, the current situation, the workers' demands, the increase in the cost of living. Previous speakers talked about tailoring salaries to the increase in the cost of living rather than always having to come back charging. Mr. Chairman, I agree with those proposals. If one looks at the current situation what does one see? Who is gaining from increases in the cost of living?
That is the question which everybody should ask instead of being satisfied with crabbing because we cannot make ends meet or of playing ostrich as this government is doing and blaming it on the world situation only to hope for better days, after studies have been made to see if prices are actually increasing. We bave reached an unbelievably ridiculous level.
Mr. Chairman, we have reached a critical point in the increasing cost of living, food, housing or money because of abusive and exhorbitant interest rates and a solution must be found as soon as possible. There are all those

Chairman, and in some financial or banking establishments, mortgage rates have reached more than 10 or 11 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, at the very moment when such an exploitation of man by finance is encouraged, 56,000 workers are told: Get back home, get back to work, you are endangering society. But for me, I say, as an out-and-out Creditist, that those who are most endangering society are those who now control the increase in the cost of living and who take advantage of it, those who control interest rates and take advantage of it. Those who are most endangering society are not those who come and demonstrate in front of Parliament, but those people who are not seen, those who play with the citizens like puppets.

Thousands of families are now doing without quality food in Canada-not in communist China-for lack of sufficient financial means when for the past few years governments have been trying obstinately to control and restrict agricultural production, for instance, going as far as penalizing dairy producers for having produced too much, and this while encouraging imports. The first thing that bothers me-and my feelings are based on the experience I acquired in the few years during which I was minister of labour-is this. Everybody who has spoken so far has been filled with good intentions and anxious to propose amendments or improvements to the bill. If each one of those amendments was accepted then I don't know one qualified arbitrator in this country who would take on the job of settling the rail dispute. They may prefer a lump sum payment. And the man who just made that remark shows he knows nothing at all about industrial relations. In recent weeks I have been involved in two labour disputes, one of which was settled by the inclusion of a cost of living clause. In the other case the membership of the union refused the inclusion of such a clause and opted for a lump sum payment instead-as you might have done, Mr. Chairman, if you had been on strike for five and a half months in British Columbia.
Let me make a point which has not been emphasized enough with regard to railroad workers, in an effort to explain what occurred here yesterday. Railway workers by their nature have always been what might be termed the aristocracy of the labour movement. This is natural because a worker in any capacity on the railway requires a particular skill; he must serve an apprenticeship and adjust to a particular environment. You cannot acquire this skill or the ability to adjust unless you work on the railway.
I was appalled in the spring of 1971 to find that a locomotive engineer operating down the Fraser Canyon earned $1800 more than my secretary who types on an IBM electric typewriter. I asked myself where our scale of values was in this particular community of ours.
At one time if you worked on the railway you were a leader in the community, you had the best wages and the best living conditions. Landlords sought you out because you had a guaranteed income. If you had worked on the railroad for 10 years you had seniority for life, and at one time a man who had 10 years' experience received a pass entitling him to travel free of charge on certain trains. Such a man had security until age 65.
That changed in the 1950's when the railways switched from steam locomotives to diesel locomotives. Shortly afterwards we saw the virtual disappearance of blacksmiths and boilermakers from the railways. Their jobs became redundant because the steam engine had outlived its usefulness. We saw patternmakers and moulders, who had

spent five years learning their profession, finding their jobs becoming obsolete and redundant. They were unable to work in other aspects of industry because of changing technology.
As a result of this the position of railway employees changed from that of importance in the community, reflected not only in stature but in wages, to a position of something less than leaders in the community. Today an electrician working for the railway might earn $4 and some cents an hour after five years' apprenticeship, covering everything from air conditioning to rewinding motors. Compare that with an electrician in the province of Quebec who, by government decree, will be paid $7.90 in 1975, plus an additional 80 cents toward his pension plan. If you were a railway worker and knew of that comparison, would you be prepared to kick in the doors of parliament? That action was not justified any more than not going back to work will be justified. If the law of the land is wrong in your individual opinion, it is still the law of the land and must be obeyed. The important thing is that we have a democracy, and this brings me to the point I really want to put forward.
On several occasions the Leader of the Opposition, who has shown concern for the working man on many occasions, has emphasized that the Conservative party would establish an industrial disputes commission which, as you know, is one of the recommendations of the Woods Task Force. I do not want to get my dates wrong again and be corrected, but I think the Woods Task Force Report was deposited during Christmas week of 1968. That commission cost the government $2 million. It was composed of leading academics and intellectual experts in the field of industrial relations.
The former leader of the NDP is smiling because he knows, as I do, that in the final analysis you do not settle labour disputes as a result of what is contained in the Woods Task Force Report; you settle them by negotiation.
All an industrial disputes commission, such as suggested by the Conservative party, would do in a democracy-and this is significant-is substitute the judgment of the Department of Labour, the judgment of the deputy minister, the judgment of the assistant deputy minister and the judgment of industrial specialists and branch heads for the judgment of the three-man board described loosely in the Woods Report as being independent.
I do not know whether the three men would be selected from the ranks of labour, but I doubt it. Perhaps two would be employers and one an employee, but more than likely they would be three academics, selected because of their experience and ability in writing on a blackboard.
In any event this commission would have access to a 30-man part-time board which no doubt would be repre sentative of the party in power. If all politicians are as partisan as I, it would contain members from their ridings. Whether they were experts in industrial relations or in some other field, they would have the responsibility of helping this three-man independent commission to substitute its judgment for that of the Department of Labour and its civil servants, and to recommend to parliament the measures it should impose upon the railway workers.

Unfortunately most of the members who come from the province of British Columbia are in the opposition, but they know the results that restrictive labour legislation breeds. Fortunately Judge Parker is no longer in British Columbia, but I suggest it will be years before labour reaction to his restrictive measures in British Columbia will disappear. I hope, for all time now, that that government has finally brought in a decent and civilized piece of labour legislation.
We are elected by the people to make unpopular decisions, and no matter what form this bill takes it will be unpopular with the railway workers of Canada. We assumed the right to stand for office and we must assume that responsibility, but we should not be prepared to cede our responsibilities, on the basis of the Woods Task Force Report, to some independent commission made up of three academics from various universities.
I could recite many statements that have appeared in editorials which condemn this type of strike action on the part of workers in industry. Many statements have been made to the effect that we cannot have strikes in essential industries. Nobody has defined an essential industry, but certainly the railways, airlines and other such industries are essential. Certainly the duties of policemen and firemen are essential.
In 1907 the then deputy minister of labour, one Mackenzie King, made the same statement the Leader of the Opposition made this morning, that when private rights become public wrongs the House of Commons must stand as a man and exercise its responsibility to the general public. It is unfortunate that in reality this legislation, which will be for the general good of the country, will work certain hardships on the unfortunate workers of the railways.
As one who has had some experience in this field I plead with members to stop playing petty politics with a piece of legislation of this importance. We should stop negotiating in respect of 8 cents or 10 cents, and 10 cents or 13 cents or something else. An hon. gentleman made a case for 13 cents, and someone else made a case for 34 cents. I could take productivity figures and make a good case for 40 cents. This will be the arbitrator's job. We do not negotiate collective agreements on the floor of the House of Commons.

The Minister of Labour is a sensitive person who represents a labour riding. Through the many years in which I have known him he has always shown great sympathy for the cause of the labour movement. If you take the legislation before us and couple it with one or two amendments-one that I recommended to the minister and one which places a limit on the time the arbitrator might take-the plight of the railway worker, for the first time in 20 years, may be recognized by the Canadian public. You fellows in the corner know you cannot have it both ways. Every time you try to have it both ways in this House of Commons-I will not say it. You fool nobody. I shall put it that way.

In answer to one question he pointed out the reason for the strike mentality, and indeed the need sometimes for entering into the strike world on the part of labour. The question was:

His answer was:

What have they done in the United States. What about the steelworkers? He refers to them, in particular in connection with compulsory arbitration, to which Secretary Brennan takes the strongest possible objection. He said:
When negotiations are going on and both sides know that a strike is possible, then more issues are forced into the open and you get better bargaining.

Under this system, if negotiations get to a stalemate, an impartial third party chosen by both sides is brought in who hears all the facts and decides on the terms of the contract.
Unions have shown this year that they can act responsibly and make this kind of bargaining work. We have been working on this kind of plan with the President's Commission for Industrial Peace. It is a much better system than passing a lot of punitive laws.

I do not know why the Leader of the Opposition, the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Labour and many others say they do not believe in compulsory arbitration, and then go ahead with it. Why the timidity? Why don't they recognize a factual situation and admit that what we are doing today is imposing an arbitrary settlement upon a group of workers and companies? Why don't they be honest and cut out all this b.s.? Why hide behind some theoretical concept of collective bargaining? We had compulsory arbitration in 1950, in 1958 when the right hon. member for Prince Albert was Prime Minister, in 1966, and we have it today. Why in hell don't we say so?
Do hon. members think that the 56,000 non-operating workers being sent back to work do not recognize this for what it is? Do they think the shop crafts, who have not yet reached the stage of being able to determine whether they will go on strike, do not recognize this for what it is? What about the running trades involved in the UTU? Do members not think they know what is happening? It is compulsory arbitration, and let's quit beating around the bush about it.
We must recognize one other fact of life. In 1950, when the first compulsory arbitration proceedings took place in this country, we destroyed the process of collective bargaining for railroad workers.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
We have a situation today where the Minister of Labour is able to stand up and say we are following the usual procedure. Of course, it is usual. It is an intrusion into free collective bargaining. We in this country and in this parliament do not want free collective bargaining to operate in the railroads, except to the extent that if a settlement can be reached without a strike or lock-out, we endorse it. The minute there is a strike or lock-out, we do not want to have anything to do with it. That is what we are doing today.
The Minister of Transport, knowledgeable as he is in the process of collective bargaining and his involvement in it, laid it right on the line. The only effective collective bargaining that takes place when there is a dispute is when there is a test of one strength against another. The strongest wins. The Minister of Transport said he had been involved in an industrial dispute and strike situation where they had an excellent case, but lost because they were weak. He gave another example where they had a poor case and won because they were strong. We are not permitting that to happen with the railroad workers.

We should quit trying to kid ourselves and everyone else. The railroad workers do not have any effective mechanism for collective bargaining. The procedures set out in the act are a myth and a sham. Yesterday, the government reinforced the position that if this parliament goes along with them on this, in any subsequent railroad negotiations it is forever committed to say, regardless of the justification of the case, whether good, bad, strong or weak, whatever the chairman of the conciliation board says, that that will be the imposed settlement. How can there be any free collective negotiations with that knowledge in the minds of the CNR and CPR?
They know full well that all they have to do is sit back, drag their feet, delay, procrastinate, and go through the mechanics of appearing before a conciliation officer. They know their case has to be made with the conciliation board chairman. No matter what the chairman says, all they have to do is be tough and that will be the settlement. What kind of collective bargaining is that? How do you classify the position of a government which says that is what it is going to impose upon the workers, a position which supports that of the companies? That is exactly what is happening.
In a normal strike situation the intention of those on strike is to create some difficulties for their employer. It is to cause a loss of production, loss of sales or some financial injury so that the employer cannot stand the losses any longer and will sit down and sign a contract. That is also the process in a lock-out. The employer causes difficulty and injury to the workers by locking them out. When the workers find it too difficult, they are willing to sign a contract. That is what collective bargaining is in a strike or lock-out situation.
In the railroad industry, the injury is not to the employer. It is to everyone but the employer. The difficulties are not experienced by the CNR or CPR. They are experienced by farmers on the Prairies who cannot ship their grain, by people in isolated communities who do not receive their shipments of goods, and by auto manufacturers who cannot get their materials in or ship their products. The difficulties are experienced by everyone but the employers. That is where parliament comes into the picture.
Regardless of all the histrionics of the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport, when an industrial dispute takes place among railroaders there is no alternative but the imposition of a settlement. The way the situation is today, there is no other agency that can do that except the parliament of Canada.
By imposing a settlement upon the workers, we are destroying free collective bargaining. It has in fact not effectively existed for the past 23 years. It was destroyed in 1950. I agree that arbitration is the only way. Does anyone have any other solution? The Babe Ruths of the negotiations, such as the hon. member for Verdun, are few and far between. Even he has outlived his usefulness in that regard.
Let us not keep up the myth about collective bargaining, how important it is and how we respect it, when every time it breaks down we discredit it more. Do members think that the railroad workers, the negotiators and the companies do not know this? We talk about the necessity of finding some other procedure. The Conservative party

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, though I do not have the credentials the hon. member for Verdun possesses in the area of negotiations between labour and management, I rise to take part in this debate as a concerned Canadian and I do speak with some knowledge of the devastating impact which this strike has had upon the Canadian economy and upon the welfare of many millions of Canadians.
I have never been involved in any labour-management negotiations but I own a business in the Town of Vegre-ville which employs some 65 persons, and I do know one thing: in order to get a fair day's work out of any individual you must reward him with a fair day's pay.
I believe the government has failed miserably in its attempt to deal with and avert this strike in an expeditious manner. I listened to the very eloquent speeches, of the hon. member for Verdun and the Minister of Transport, who attempted to explain away the government's position in relation to the strike. They attempted to tell this House the reason the strike came about, but I should like to state that they failed to convince me. This government failed to expedite a satisfactory solution to the problems which led to this strike.
It is the responsibility and the job of the Minister of Transport to see that goods and people move uninterruptedly in this country, and I suggest he should take stock of his position in relation to this strike.
We are assembled here this afternoon to restore services in Canada which are not only essential but which represent a national lifeline. The cost of this disruption and its effect on our economy has amounted to untold millions of dollars, and the government cannot continue to ignore the situation. This strike has caused a great deal of suffering, discomfort and misery to millions of people.
We are lucky that the provinces of Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island have shown such generosity, kindness and hospitality. The residents of those two islands have opened their doors and their hearts to the thousands of people stranded there. I must commend the provincial governments and the service clubs, particularly the Lions and the Kinsmen, for the admirable job they have done in helping to overcome the hardships and misery caused by this strike. These organizations and the two governments are to be commended for their outward kindness in accommodating these unfortunate victims.
The innocent victims of this strike have no recourse; they can take no action against anyone. If strikes are to be a way of life in this country perhaps it is time to consider ways and means by which innocent victims, who are detrimentally affected by a work stoppage, can take action against the unions, management, or both.
We have had too many strikes in this country, particularly in essential services. Many services have been interrupted; services which are fundamental and necessary to the orderly functioning of our economy and our society. Most of these services enjoy a monopolistic position because we are provided with no alternative. This has caused corporations, small businesses, farmers, and many others untold hardship and financial loss. Transportation is indeed in this category.
IThe Assistant Deputy Chairman.]
This country is fed up to the teeth with strikes. The people have had their fill and are demanding alternative methods to the negotiating process. As far as many Canadians are concerned a strike is an obsolete and archaic tool. I understand there are something of the order of 54 strikes taking place in our nation at the present time, and a number of others pending. These will involve thousands of people.
There has been a void of action on the part of this and former Liberal governments to grapple with new devices or techniques which would be more effective in dealing with management-labour disputes. This is especially true in respect of essential services. What has this government done to improve the bargaining process? What has it done to protect the public from disruption of essential services? What has it done since the last legislation in 1966? I suggest the answer is nothing.
When the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson introduced the back-to-work legislation in 1966 he said, as reported at page 7771 of Hansard for August 29 of that year:
We must find better methods for the negotiation and settlement of disputes in the railway industry, and in other industries; new and improved mediation and conciliation procedures which will take into account new circumstances, new conditions in industrial society; which will more effectively preserve the right of the employee in these new conditions and also adequately protect the national interest, particularly in respect of essential national services.
This government has failed to act or live up to that commitment made by a respected Liberal leader who, I am sure, made that statement in good faith.
What is to be done about future strikes in essential services and future disruptions in transportation? Does the government intend to go along merrily as it has in the past, reacting to each crisis as it happens? Does it intend to continue to act in this way in respect of disruptions in airline service and the service provided by longshoremen and grain handlers, ignoring the fact that this is all part of a larger problem? Or is the government prepared to present to parliament a program to provide for better ways and means of negotiating, in order that the public can be protected against the devastating and damaging effects of strikes in essential services?
Our party has put forward a proposal which I think marks the beginning of a new mechanism. It has been outlined by my leader and by the hon. member for St. John's East. I will not go into detail, but it could be the starting point of a new approach to labour-management disputes, and I hope the government is prepared to give it serious consideration. The government has been known to borrow our ideas in the past and I am sure we will not mind if it does so in the future, particularly, if this will serve the public interest. Perhaps a parliamentary committee should consider the Woods Report and other factors in an attempt to find ways and means for the better settlement of disputes. This government and this parliament should consider this issue immediately.
When considering a public industrial disputes commission it should be noted that it is essential to the proposal that workers in essential services receive fair and just payment. I believe an appropriate pay scale must be established. If the non-op railway workers are considered to be essential workers they must be paid on that basis, just as
August 31, 1973

we pay policemen and firemen in this country on the basis of the essential services they perform.
Many hon. members have alluded to the fact that railway workers perform an essential service. There can be no doubt about that fact. Those employees who are a part of this network must be treated as essential employees. We must ensure that they receive a decent income for their labours, decent working conditions, adequate security, decent pensions and so on.
Furthermore, I believe management and the unions must be encouraged to commence their bargaining process at a much earlier date. Under the existing framework there is too much opportunity to play around rather than bargain meaningfully before the expiration of the contract. This is tantamount to playing a game with the public, all of which is devastating and costly. I believe that appropriate incentives could be put in place to encourage the expedition of the bargaining process prior to the expiration of a contract. These are just a few ideas, but they are ideas which I believe the government can consider.
I am sure there are many other ideas which could be brought forth. The point I want to reiterate very strongly is the fact that we must address ourselves to establishing a much better system of collective bargaining, and a much better system to overcome labour-management disputes in essential services.
I believe it is precisely because of the incompetence of this government in the area of labour unrest, and its poor record in respect of economic management, inflation and the cost of living, that we are presently in a climate of confused economic chaos. Previously I said I believe the people of Canada are fed up with strikes. I want to say, however, that they are also fed up with this government. They are fed up with the economic mess we have at the present time. They are fed up with the deterioration in labour relations. They are fed up because of the government's inaction in respect of averting the strike we are now legislating during this special sitting of the House.
The government was forewarned regarding the implications long before the strike occurred. I am one who believes this strike could have been avoided. I am sure it could have been avoided with a settlement as good as the strikers will receive as a result of this legislation and the negotiation and mediation which follows thereafter.
I do not believe the government accepted its proper responsibility in July. I think we could have moved to settle this strike before the House adjourned in July. On July 26, for example, when the first round of rotating strikes occurred, the hon. member for St. John's East asked the Minister of Labour a question about the strike and the Minister of Labour failed to even recognize that a strike was on our hands. He referred to it merely as a temporary walkout. This is recorded at page 5984 of Hansard. This is an example of sheer incompetence.
What has happened? Grain deliveries have been disastrously affected. Our reputation as a supplier of grain has again become tarnished. Because of additional carrying charges, because of additional demurrage charges, and plugged elevator systems there is less money for the pro-
Railway Operations Act
ducer. We are now in the midst of the harvest season and the elevator system is plugged because of the railway strike. In the area of livestock the ill-conceived implementation of the export restrictions in respect of beef and pork, which sent thousands of cattle back to farms which originally were destined for market, coupled with rail strikes, has complicated the orderly marketing process of cattle and hogs.
This was a very costly error on the part of the government. Untold millions have been lost in the livestock industry and in the grain industry, the two main industries of western Canada. There is a backlog of processed meat. Cattle are being bought in quantities of one, two, three of four, rather than in hundreds and thousands. The manufacturing industry is being paralysed. Huge lay-offs are being experienced in our communities in western Canada. The merchants are without shoes and clothing to sell. This situation exists not only in western Canada but in central Canada as well.
Then there is the matter of repair parts for machinery and equipment. This has an effect on the harvest. Farmers are unable to buy repair parts in order to keep their machinery in operation. This situation could have been anticipated long before the strike occurred. We are now faced with a gasoline shortage. Even if the trains begin to roll on Monday we could still experience a temporary gasoline shortage which would affect the harvesting operation. This is a matter of life and death because one must take advantage of harvest weather when it is present.
All across this country the detrimental effect of the strike has been recorded. What did the Minister of Transport do during the period leading up to the strike? His expertise in labour-management negotiations has been mentioned previously. Did he exercise his responsibility? Did he use his force and sheer determination to encourage the parties to get together and settle this strike before it actually occurred? I do not know, but I did not gather from his speech this afternoon that he undertook his task in a responsible manner. Perhaps he has been as ineffective here as in mapping out a new national transportation policy.
This is an area in which some radical changes and approaches might be mapped out, rather than the piecemeal approach that was taken at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. We also wonder about the role of the CNR and Air Canada that was alluded to by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East. These two bodies have not been scrutinized by the parliamentary committee.
We are told that Air Canada is operating as a rudderless ship. I should like to know more about the operation of the CNR and Air Canada, but the minister and the government have denied the members of the House an opportunity to examine the officials of these two large Crown corporations. We wonder why the minister has denied the members of the House an opportunity to examine the annual accounts for the years 1971 and 1972. We wonder why there has been a refusal to come clean in respect of the Air Canada financing bill. We wonder why we have not been able to get the management side of the story. If we did, perhaps we would all be in a much better position

August 31, 1973
Railway Operations Act
to deal in a more objective way with the total impact of this particular dispute.
We note that the net income of the Canadian railways, as reported by Statistics Canada, has more than doubled in the first four months of 1973. Perhaps this may have some bearing on the kind of settlement to which the non-ops are entitled.
The members of this House have been denied an opportunity to cross-examine the officials of these institutions. We would also like to know what has happened in respect of the promised freight rate freeze that had been alluded to by the minister in his outburst at the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. These are some of the answers we seek.
I see you are on the edge of your seat, Mr. Chairman, and therefore I shall be very brief. In my opinion parliament and the people of Canada have been cheated by this minister who has refused to allow these two Crown corporations, each of which provides an essential service, to be scrutinized by a parliamentary committee.
It is for that reason that we are somewhat suspicious, and that we lay the result of this strike primarily on the doorstep of this government. It is mainly due to the government's incompetence and the devious manner in which it has handled transportation matters in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am a neophyte in the House and I as a newcomer here and as a spectator of this sport I have listened, read and tried to find out what is going on. I also happen to have a very large group of non ops and running tradesmen on railroads in my riding. So I decided to take a look at Hansard of the period when similar legislation was introduced in the House.
After reading Hansard for August 29, 1966 and after listening to the speeches that have been made in the House yesterday and today, I must say that I have never heard such phoney, hollow speeches, and such verbiage as I have heard thrown around here by the Liberals and Conservatives. I want to give an instance of this. The Conservatives have been clamouring for the return of the workers to their jobs since the rotating strikes started. When I look back at Hansard for August 29, 1966,1 see that the former leader of that party, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, as recorded at page 7733 of Hansard, had the following to say:
I recall very well that debate in 1950.
He was referring to similar legislation in 1950, the first instance of compulsory arbitration imposed by parliament on the railway workers. He went on to say:
The attitude then taken by the Conservative party was that in so far as compulsory arbitration was concerned the party was against it, and members of this party voted accordingly when a vote took place on the motion made by the then prime minister.
So it seems that the Conservative party had taken a position against compulsory arbitration. I hear them in the House today advocating that. They have advocated it since July 26, 1973, when the rotating strikes started.
I have listened to my leader. He said that every court should have a jester. I suppose every parliament should

have a Pontius Pilate. I think it is remarkable that the Minister of Transport should tell members in the House that we are not here to solve the dispute, we are here to solve the emergency, and that we are not all cognizant of the material, the information, and the statistics involved in this dispute.
Why are we elected by the people of Canada if we are not to inform ourselves and become knowledgeable of the kind of legislation that we are expected to debate and to pass? I suggest to you that members of the House are not now familiar with the demands of the non-ops and the arguments of the companies, which have been few and far between because the companies have not negotiated fairly and in good faith. Surely then members are not justified in sitting in the House if they have not informed themselves on those matters. They should have done their homework, and it is obvious that they have not.
The hon. member for Verdun made a comparison, which I found funny, between the salary of an engineer on the railroad and that of his secretary. He said that she was making $1,800 less than the engineer. I suggest that if he had any sort of social conscience he should have organized the secretaries so that they would not be making $1,800 less than the organized workers.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Transport this morning. Indeed he is eloquent, and I would compare him in many ways with the hon. member for Verdun because in fact they are the only two members sitting on that side of the House who have any knowledge of or sympathy for the working people of this country. It is revealing indeed that the Minister of Transport was called upon by the Liberals to bail them out, and obviously the Conservatives in this particular instance will also be bailed out by that speech in which the minister said that we are not in a position to make a decision. It seems to me that once parliament took the option of bringing in legislation to put the workers back to work to end the emergency, the onus is on parliament to make sure that the emergency is ended and that the workers have a fair and just wage on which to live.

I do not call that politicking because I have listened to members on that side of the House, and to the Liberal members in my area. Incidentally, there are no Conservatives in northern Ontario. I have listened to the Liberals stand up before the non-ops in the last three or four days and tell them: "We agree that what you are asking is fair and just. We agree with your wage demands. They are not out of line. We agree with your desire for job security. It is what every other worker in industry has. You are not asking for anything that is out of line".
Now they come and support a bill which gives the workers what the company offered last Monday, and which the union turned down. I find that false because at election time both the Tories and the Liberals stood up and pretended that they were the friends of the workers. If they are the friends of the workers, why do they not on this occasion, instead of saying all these words which are empty and hollow, accept the Weldon report and give the workers a fair and just settlement? Why do they engage in the parrying of empty, fancy words back and forth? It seems to me that it is time the workers realized that the
August 31, 1973

two old line parties are closely allied with business and will never bring in a decision in favour of the workers.

speechtext:
This has been so ever since 1950. I know you are upset about this. The hon. member for Peel South is very upset. I can understand the fact that he is upset because I am sure the workers will note how he and his colleagues voted last night, and they will note how they will vote on our amendments. I hope they will carry the message to other workers throughout the highly industrialized areas such as the cities of Hamilton and Windsor so that the workers know how the Conservatives and Liberals are voting when it comes to a crunch between management and workers.
The Minister of Labour in his press release on August 30 stated in his preamble regarding the strike:
This strike . . . has resulted in widespread economic loss to the extent that the welfare of the nation has become imperilled.
As the Prime Minister has indicated, it is essential to the interests of the people of Canada, and the welfare of our nation, that railway operations be resumed immediately.
The minister echoes what was said in 1966 and before that in 1950.
Indeed, this whole scenario which is now unfolding has been played before. One has only to pick up the Hansard of 1966 and read the same script again. It is interesting to note that one year it is the Liberals who are imposing compulsory arbitration and the Tories who are screaming against it, and then it is the Tories who are pushing compulsory arbitration down the throats of the workers while the Liberals slither into the role of pretended opposition. It is precisely this kind of situation which demonstrates that there is absolutely no difference between these two groups. They are identical in all but name, and I strongly suspect that the only reason the members on both sides of the House have not merged is that they enjoy having someone who agrees to argue with them.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext: Let's talk about British Columbia.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
There is no strike going on in British Columbia at the moment.
Let us get back to the Minister of Labour's statement. He stated that the welfare of the nation is in peril. In the last few weeks we have been told that the economy is suffering and the general public is suffering. This, obviously, is true. We are told that the government must legislate the workers back to work, because they are essential. Actually, I have never heard the words "essential service" used so often as in the last two days. If they are so essential, and it seems that they only become essential when they remove their services from their employers, why, in heaven's name, are they not given a fair wage and job security?
Members here enjoy a fair wage but do not enjoy security. Do hon. members think of these essential workers between contracts? No. When the non-ops are doing their job day after day, year after year, do the two old time parties ever pause to wonder if these essential workers
Railway Operations Act
have enough money to feed and shelter their families and keep up with the rising cost of living, which has run amok in this country? I doubt it.
The simplistic solution of wage and price controls brings no guarantees for workers earning poor wages. Do the two parties ever think about the growing insecurity which these essential workers face through the ever-increasing encroachment of technology on their jobs. I think not. And I do not believe for a minute that parliament has been recalled because the Liberals are concerned about the welfare of the nation or the interests of the Canadian people. After all, it was not so long ago that the Minister of Finance sauntered out of his summer retreat to announce to an angry and concerned public that prices are hurting, but that's not enough to recall parliament. And this is where deception of the most gross and despicable nature is being perpetrated on the Canadian people. The Liberals name the villain, act out a little parliamentary voodoo, and then declare the demon exorcised.
Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, we observed a demonstration by the rail workers. Those rail workers have been cast in the same role over the years, albeit reluctantly. They know they have always been screwed by the government and they know they are about to be screwed again. They know why they were demonstrating outside the House of Commons. They know why we are here. They were here because they believed that the members of parliament who are in this House, and who are their representatives, are not going to give them a fair settlement, and they were correct. They knew the situation, knew what they were to be offered, and they were absolutely correct.
I say that when this government exercises its prerogative to recall parliament and get the workers back to work, back to their jobs, the responsibility rests with the government to make absolutely certain that those workers receive a just settlement. This government is not and should not be in the business of strike breaking, and it should not be in servitude to the companies.

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext: What would you do?

subtopic: MAINTENANCE OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS ACT, MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION OF OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTES
speechtext:
We would give the workers a just and decent wage, so that they could keep up with the increasing cost of living. It is clear that the rail workers are only asking for what is fair and just. Their demands clearly are not exorbitant.
Surely no member in this House can say that what these men are asking is exorbitant and inflationary. Indeed, it is the policies of provincial Tories and federal Liberals which have led to the inflationary spiral which has put these men behind the eight ball. It is obvious that their fringe benefit packages cannot begin to approach those of workers in other comparable industries, and I could give you comparisons.
In the Sudbury area the major employers are Inco and Falconbridge. The union employees of those two large companies have worked out a medical and dental plan, and there is a company pension. The non-ops do not have those things. The average wage of the Inco or Falconbridge workers is $5.75 per hour. I think the non ops get $3.54 per hour. On the other hand the stores in the area that serve the workers of Inco and Falconbridge base their prices on

August 31, 1973
Railway Operations Act
the high wages, and not on the average wage of $3.54 paid to the non-ops.
These men have their backs to the wall. If you think that this legislation will end the emergency on the railways, you have another think coming, because the bookings off will continue, as will the harassment, and members here will have contributed to the broken spirit of the railroad workers. As I said, the fringe benefit packages of these workers cannot begin to approach the benefits of workers in comparable industries. Nor can it be said that they do not deserve sick leave and pension plan improvements.
It is true that the non-ops are in jeopardy because of advancing technology, and it is only fair that they have some provision for security. It is also true that the rail workers have been more than patient with the companies and the government. It has been 19 months since the last wage increase was granted. So, I think they have been more than patient. Further, they have no strike benefits. It has also become evident that the companies have not bargained in good faitn. Actually, the deputy minister went on television the other night and said that the companies have not bargained in good faith.
I say, let us string the companies, so that they will always bargain in good faith in the future and perhaps we will not need to be unfair to the workers.
How can the government come up with such an objectionable, useless mess of nothing as Bill C-217? This bill offers the workers nothing. This bill attempts to give the workers exactly what they had turned down in negotiations, because they knew it was not sufficient. It waxes strange indeed that this government not only permits but encourages Canadian National railways, which belongs to the working people of this country, to operate as badly as a private corporation, instead of setting a standard for rail workers, instead of leading the way for fair and just and respectable settlements in Canada. Instead, there has been collusion, and the companies have brought forward this mess of pottage that we see reflected in Bill C-217.
Do the Liberals honestly think that this bill will bring peace and harmony to the labour situation? Where have they been for the last nine months. Workers have been booking off. I raised the issue in this House as early as the beginning of July, and the bookings off had been taking place for the previous three months. I predict, Mr. Chairman, that this unrest on the railroads will continue. The rail workers have been displaying dissatisfaction over the last nine months with the offers the companies have been making. They have been fed up with the fact that after nine months they have no contract. Where were the Liberals during those selective strikes? What were they doing during the rail disruptions and the bookings off?

the Department of Labour and the Liberal cabinet. The history of settlements forced on the workers, at times when Liberals or Tories were in charge of legislation to put workers back to work, might be compared with putting Dracula in charge of the Red Cross blood banks!
